questions.stem: Under Treasury Circular 230, a practitioner who learns that a client has not complied with the federal tax laws or has made an error in a previously filed return must:

options.text: Promptly advise the client of the noncompliance, error, or omission and of the consequences of not correcting it
Withdraw from the engagement and refuse to prepare any further returns
Immediately notify the IRS of the client's noncompliance
Amend the prior return without the client's consent to avoid penalties

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Circular 230 §10.21 requires a practitioner who knows of a client's error or omission to advise the client of it and of the consequences of not correcting it; the decision to correct rests with the client. Why the others are wrong: **C** the practitioner owes a duty of confidentiality and may not report the client to the IRS; **B** withdrawal is not mandated by the rule; **D** the practitioner cannot amend or disclose without the client's consent.

questions.stem: A CPA prepares a return taking a position that a reasonable tax practitioner would conclude has roughly a 20% likelihood of being sustained on its merits. The position is not disclosed and is not a tax shelter. Under the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services, may the CPA recommend the position?

options.text: No, because every undisclosed position must satisfy the 'more likely than not' standard
No, because an undisclosed position generally requires at least a 'substantial authority' or 'realistic possibility' level of support
Yes, because the position meets the 'realistic possibility of success' standard
Yes, because any position with a colorable basis may be taken without disclosure

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** SSTS No. 1 lets a CPA recommend an undisclosed, non-shelter position only if it meets the applicable reporting standard — generally substantial authority or at least a realistic possibility of success (about one-in-three); a 20% position falls short and should be disclosed. Why the others are wrong: **A** the more-likely-than-not (>50%) standard applies to tax shelters, not every position; **C** realistic possibility is roughly one-in-three, which 20% does not meet; **D** a mere colorable/reasonable basis suffices only when the position is disclosed.

questions.stem: A taxpayer disputes proposed adjustments and ultimately litigates without prepaying the tax. Place these stages of the federal tax controversy process in chronological order.

options.text: IRS examination (audit) of the return and proposed adjustments
Administrative appeal to the IRS Appeals Office (30-day letter)
Issuance of a statutory notice of deficiency (90-day letter)
Filing a petition in the U.S. Tax Court

questions.explanation: The controversy generally proceeds in this order: the IRS first examines the return and proposes adjustments; the taxpayer may then pursue an administrative appeal to the Appeals Office (typically after a 30-day letter); if unresolved, the IRS issues a statutory notice of deficiency (90-day letter); and to litigate without first paying the tax, the taxpayer files a petition in the U.S. Tax Court within 90 days of that notice. Skipping ahead is not possible because each step is triggered by the prior one — the 90-day letter is the 'ticket' to Tax Court.

questions.stem: An individual taxpayer files an accurate return but, due to a math error in their favor, understates tax. The IRS assesses an accuracy-related penalty for a substantial understatement of income tax. For an individual, a 'substantial understatement' generally exists when the understatement exceeds:

options.text: A flat $1,000 regardless of the tax shown
5% of adjusted gross income
The greater of 25% of the tax required to be shown, or $10,000
The greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown, or $5,000

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Under IRC §6662, an individual's understatement is 'substantial' if it exceeds the greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000, triggering the 20% accuracy-related penalty. Why the others are wrong: **C** the 25%/$10,000 figures do not state the individual threshold; **A** there is no flat $1,000 trigger; **B** the test is based on the tax required to be shown, not a percentage of AGI.

questions.stem: A paid tax return preparer takes an unreasonable position on a client's return. The position lacks substantial authority and was not disclosed, but the preparer had no reasonable basis and the understatement was not willful. Under IRC §6694(a), the first-tier preparer penalty is generally the greater of $1,000 or:

options.text: 50% of the income the preparer derived (or to be derived) from preparing the return
100% of the understatement of tax
75% of the income the preparer derived from preparing the return
10% of the client's total tax liability

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The §6694(a) penalty for an unreasonable position is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived (or to be derived) by the preparer from the return. Why the others are wrong: **C** 75% of the preparer's income applies to the §6694(b) penalty for willful or reckless conduct, not the first tier; **B** the penalty is measured by the preparer's fee, not the full understatement; **D** there is no 10%-of-client-liability preparer penalty.

questions.stem: Under Treasury Circular 230, which two practices are expressly prohibited or restricted for practitioners? (Select two.)

options.text: Charging an unconscionable fee for representing a client before the IRS
Returning a client's records to the client upon request when there is a fee dispute
Charging a contingent fee for preparing an original tax return, except in limited circumstances
Advising a client about the tax consequences of a transaction the client is considering

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Circular 230 §10.27 forbids unconscionable fees and generally bars contingent fees for preparing original returns (allowing them only in limited situations such as certain refund claims or IRS examinations). Why the others are wrong: **B** §10.28 requires the practitioner to return a client's own records even amid a fee dispute, so refusing would be the violation; **D** advising a client on the tax consequences of a contemplated transaction is a core, permitted service.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to substantiate a charitable contribution of $300 cash made to a qualified organization. To deduct the gift, the taxpayer must, at a minimum, keep:

options.text: A qualified written appraisal of the donated amount
A bank record or written communication from the charity showing the name, date, and amount of the contribution
Form 8283 attached to the return regardless of the gift's size
Nothing, because cash contributions under $500 require no records

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Any cash charitable contribution requires a bank record or a written communication from the charity showing its name, the date, and the amount; gifts of $250 or more also need a contemporaneous written acknowledgment. Why the others are wrong: **A** even small cash gifts need a record — there is no exemption; **C** appraisals are for noncash gifts over $5,000; **D** Form 8283 is for noncash contributions over $500, not cash.

questions.stem: A principal privately tells her agent not to buy goods on credit, but the agent has openly purchased on credit for the principal for years and third parties know this. The agent again buys goods on credit from a longtime supplier who is unaware of the new restriction. Is the principal bound?

options.text: No, because an agent can never bind a principal once actual authority is withdrawn
Yes, but only if the agent also had express written authority
Yes, because the agent had apparent authority based on the principal's prior conduct
No, because the principal expressly revoked the agent's actual authority

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Apparent authority arises from the principal's manifestations to third parties; having let the agent buy on credit for years, the principal is bound to a supplier who reasonably relied without knowing of the secret restriction. Why the others are wrong: **A** apparent authority can still bind the principal after actual authority ends; **B** apparent authority needs no written grant — it flows from the principal's conduct; **D** revoking actual authority does not by itself end apparent authority as to unaware third parties.

questions.stem: Under the UCC, a merchant emails another merchant a signed offer to sell goods, stating the offer 'will remain open for 60 days.' No consideration is paid for this promise. After 20 days, before any acceptance, the offeror tries to revoke. Is the revocation effective?

options.text: No, because the firm offer is irrevocable for the full 60 days and consideration is required to revoke
Yes, because firm offers apply only to contracts for services
Yes, because without consideration any offer is freely revocable
No, because a firm offer is irrevocable for the stated period, but in no event longer than three months

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** UCC §2-205 makes a merchant's signed written offer irrevocable for the time stated without consideration, but never longer than three months; 20 days into a 60-day promise it is still firm, so the revocation fails. Why the others are wrong: **C** the firm-offer rule dispenses with consideration; **A** no consideration is needed and the cap is three months; **B** Article 2 firm offers cover the sale of goods, not services.

questions.stem: A creditor holds a surety's guarantee for a $50,000 debt. Without the surety's consent, the creditor and the principal debtor agree to materially increase the interest rate and extend the due date. What is the effect on a gratuitous (uncompensated) surety?

options.text: The surety is completely discharged because a material modification was made without consent
The surety's liability increases to match the higher interest rate automatically
The surety remains fully liable because sureties are always bound regardless of modifications
The surety is liable only for the original principal but not relieved of the guarantee

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A material modification of the underlying obligation made without the surety's consent discharges an uncompensated (gratuitous) surety entirely, because it changes the bargained-for risk. Why the others are wrong: **B** the surety never agreed to the higher rate, so liability does not silently expand; **C** sureties are not bound through unconsented material changes; **D** a gratuitous surety is fully discharged, not merely capped at the original principal.

questions.stem: An issuer sells securities solely to accredited investors in an unlimited dollar amount, engages in no general solicitation, and provides any information the investors request. Which Securities Act of 1933 registration exemption is the issuer most likely relying on?

options.text: Regulation A, Tier 1
Regulation D, Rule 506(b)
Section 11 of the 1933 Act
Rule 10b-5 under the 1934 Act

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Rule 506(b) of Regulation D permits raising an unlimited amount from unlimited accredited investors (plus up to 35 sophisticated non-accredited investors) with no general solicitation. Why the others are wrong: **A** Regulation A is a capped mini-registration, not an unlimited private placement; **C** Section 11 is a liability provision for false registration statements, not an exemption; **D** Rule 10b-5 is the 1934 Act antifraud rule, not a registration exemption.

questions.stem: Which characteristic is a defining feature of a general partnership?

options.text: Formation requires filing articles of organization with the state
The partnership pays federal income tax at the entity level
Each general partner has unlimited personal liability for partnership debts
Partners have limited liability up to their capital contributions

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A hallmark of a general partnership is that every general partner is jointly and severally liable, with unlimited personal exposure, for partnership debts. Why the others are wrong: **A** a general partnership can form with no state filing, unlike an LLC or corporation; **B** a partnership is a pass-through and pays no entity-level federal income tax; **D** limited liability up to contributions describes limited partners, LLC members, or shareholders.

questions.stem: A buyer and seller have a written contract for the sale of 1,000 widgets. The buyer later orally agrees to a quantity change to 1,500 widgets; nothing is put in writing. The total price now exceeds $500. Under UCC Article 2, is the modification enforceable?

options.text: Yes, because UCC modifications never require consideration and are always enforceable
No, because all contract modifications require new consideration under the UCC
Yes, because oral modifications to written contracts are always permitted under the UCC
No, because the contract as modified is within the Statute of Frauds and the increased quantity is not evidenced by a writing

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** UCC modifications need no consideration, but a modified goods contract within the Statute of Frauds ($500 or more) must satisfy the writing requirement; the unwritten increase to 1,500 widgets is unenforceable. Why the others are wrong: **A** lack of consideration is fine, but the Statute of Frauds still applies; **B** the UCC does not require consideration to modify a goods contract; **C** oral modification is not always allowed when the modified deal must be in writing.

questions.stem: A secured party perfects a purchase-money security interest (PMSI) in inventory. To have priority over an earlier-perfected general security interest in the same inventory, the PMSI secured party must, before the debtor receives the inventory:

options.text: Perfect the PMSI and send an authenticated notification to the holder of the conflicting security interest
Obtain the debtor's written promise not to grant other security interests
Take possession of the entire inventory until the loan is repaid
Merely file a financing statement within 20 days after the debtor receives the inventory

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For PMSI priority in inventory, Article 9 requires the secured party to perfect (file) before the debtor takes possession and to send an authenticated notification to existing conflicting secured parties before delivery. Why the others are wrong: **C** the 20-day grace period applies to PMSIs in non-inventory goods like equipment; **D** a debtor's negative promise does not create priority; **B** possession is not how an inventory PMSI is perfected.

questions.stem: Which two elements are required to form a valid, enforceable contract under the common law? (Select two.)

options.text: A writing signed by both parties, regardless of subject matter
A valid offer and acceptance (mutual assent)
Notarization by a licensed notary public
Consideration (a bargained-for exchange)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** Common-law contract formation requires mutual assent (offer and acceptance) and consideration, along with capacity and legality. Why the others are wrong: **A** a signed writing is required only for contracts within the Statute of Frauds, not every contract; **C** notarization is never a general requirement for contract validity.

questions.stem: Under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which type of issuer is generally subject to the periodic reporting requirements (Forms 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K)?

options.text: Only companies conducting an initial public offering under the 1933 Act
A company whose securities are traded on a national exchange or that has more than a threshold number of holders and total assets
Only foreign private issuers, but never domestic companies
Any sole proprietorship with gross revenue over $1 million

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The 1934 Act imposes ongoing periodic reporting on issuers listed on a national exchange or that meet the §12 asset/holder thresholds. Why the others are wrong: **A** the 1933 Act governs the offering's registration, while the 1934 Act governs ongoing reporting; **C** domestic reporting companies are squarely covered, not just foreign private issuers; **D** a sole proprietorship with no registered securities is not a reporting company.

questions.stem: A donor gives a parent stock with a basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $25,000 at the date of the gift. No gift tax is paid. If the donee later sells the stock, what basis is used to determine the donee's loss?

options.text: The average of the donor's basis and the fair market value, $32,500
Zero, because gifted property has no loss basis
$25,000, the fair market value at the date of the gift
$40,000, the donor's carryover basis

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** When gifted property's FMV is below the donor's basis, the dual-basis rule uses FMV at the gift date ($25,000) to compute a loss, preventing the donee from claiming the donor's pre-gift decline. Why the others are wrong: **D** the $40,000 carryover basis is used to compute a gain, not a loss; **A** no averaging rule exists; **B** gifted property does have a loss basis — it is simply the lower FMV figure.

questions.stem: An heir inherits land from a decedent. The decedent's adjusted basis was $100,000; the fair market value on the date of death was $250,000, and the executor does not elect the alternate valuation date. What is the heir's basis in the land?

options.text: Zero until the heir sells the property
$100,000, the decedent's carryover adjusted basis
$175,000, the average of basis and fair market value
$250,000, the fair market value on the date of death (stepped-up basis)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to its FMV on the date of death (here $250,000), a 'stepped-up' basis under IRC §1014. Why the others are wrong: **B** the decedent's carryover basis applies to gifts, not inheritances; **C** no averaging rule applies; **A** the heir has a basis immediately upon inheritance, not only at sale.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells equipment used in a trade or business for $30,000. The equipment was purchased for $50,000 and $35,000 of depreciation had been taken, giving an adjusted basis of $15,000. How is the $15,000 gain characterized under Section 1245?

options.text: $15,000 is ordinary income because it does not exceed the depreciation taken
$15,000 is tax-exempt because the asset was sold at a loss relative to cost
$15,000 is Section 1231 gain eligible for capital treatment
$15,000 is long-term capital gain

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Section 1245 recaptures gain as ordinary income up to the lesser of the gain ($15,000) or depreciation taken ($35,000); the entire $15,000 gain is within the depreciation, so all of it is ordinary income. Why the others are wrong: **C** it is not long-term capital gain to the extent of recapture; **B** §1231 treatment applies only to gain beyond §1245 recapture, of which there is none; **D** there is a realized gain ($30,000 over $15,000 basis), so it is taxable.

questions.stem: An investor exchanges real property held for investment (basis $80,000) for other like-kind investment real property worth $120,000 and also receives $20,000 of cash boot. The exchange otherwise qualifies under Section 1031. How much gain is recognized?

options.text: $40,000, the difference between the new property's value and the old basis
$20,000, the lesser of the realized gain or the boot received
$0, because all like-kind exchanges are fully tax-free
$60,000, the entire realized gain

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In a §1031 exchange, gain is recognized to the extent of boot received but not more than the realized gain. Realized gain is $60,000 ($140,000 received − $80,000 basis); recognized gain is limited to the $20,000 boot. Why the others are wrong: **D** the full $60,000 is deferred except for the boot; **C** boot triggers some recognition, so it is not fully tax-free; **A** $40,000 is not a recognition measure under §1031.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are generally excluded from an individual's gross income? (Select two.)

options.text: Life insurance proceeds received by reason of the insured's death
Interest on a state or municipal bond
Wages reported on Form W-2
Gambling winnings from a casino

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Life insurance proceeds paid because of the insured's death (IRC §101) and interest on state or municipal bonds (IRC §103) are both excluded from gross income. Why the others are wrong: **C** wages are classic includible compensation; **D** gambling winnings are fully includible in gross income.

questions.stem: An unmarried taxpayer maintains a home that is the principal residence for more than half the year of her dependent child, and she pays more than half the cost of keeping up the home. Which filing status is most advantageous and available to her?

options.text: Married filing separately
Qualifying surviving spouse
Single
Head of household

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Head of household applies to an unmarried (or considered-unmarried) taxpayer who pays more than half the cost of a home that is the principal residence of a qualifying person (such as a dependent child) for more than half the year. Why the others are wrong: **B** single status is available but less favorable; **A** qualifying surviving spouse needs a spouse who died in one of the two prior years; **C** MFS requires being married and is generally least favorable.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual pays $6,000 in health insurance premiums for herself and reports a net profit on Schedule C. She is not eligible for any employer-subsidized health plan. How is the premium most appropriately treated?

options.text: As an above-the-line deduction (adjustment) to arrive at AGI, limited to net self-employment earnings
As a fully refundable tax credit equal to the premiums paid
As an itemized medical deduction subject to the 7.5%-of-AGI floor only
As a nondeductible personal expense

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The self-employed health insurance deduction is an above-the-line adjustment to income, limited to the taxpayer's net earnings from self-employment, available when not eligible for subsidized employer coverage. Why the others are wrong: **C** treating it only as an itemized medical expense ignores the available above-the-line deduction; **B** it is a deduction, not a refundable credit; **D** it is deductible, not a nondeductible personal expense.

questions.stem: A taxpayer actively participates in a rental real estate activity and has a $30,000 loss for the year. The taxpayer's modified AGI is $90,000 and has no other passive income. Under the active-participation rental real estate exception, how much of the loss may the taxpayer generally deduct against nonpassive income?

options.text: $12,500, because the allowance is always halved
$25,000, the maximum special allowance for active participants at this income level
$30,000, the entire loss, because active participation removes all passive limits
$0, because rental real estate losses are always fully suspended

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The active-participation exception allows up to a $25,000 special allowance of rental real estate losses against nonpassive income, phasing out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified AGI, so at $90,000 the full $25,000 is available. Why the others are wrong: **A** the $12,500 reduced cap applies to married filing separately taxpayers; **C** the allowance caps the deduction at $25,000, suspending the remaining $5,000; **D** the exception is precisely what permits a current deduction.

questions.stem: During the year, an employer provides an employee with $60,000 of group-term life insurance coverage as a tax-free fringe benefit. How much of this coverage, if any, generally produces taxable income to the employee?

options.text: The entire $60,000 of coverage is tax-free with no limit
The full premium for all $60,000 is taxable to the employee
The cost (per IRS tables) of coverage exceeding $50,000 is includible in income
Only coverage exceeding $100,000 is taxable

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Under IRC §79, employer-provided group-term life insurance is excludable up to $50,000 of coverage; the cost (computed using IRS Table I) of coverage above $50,000 is taxable to the employee. Why the others are wrong: **A** the exclusion is capped at $50,000; **B** only the excess coverage's table cost — not the full premium — is taxable; **D** the threshold is $50,000, not $100,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the tax treatment of qualified dividends received by an individual?

options.text: Always taxed at the taxpayer's ordinary income tax rates
Completely excluded from gross income
Subject only to self-employment tax
Taxed at preferential long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20%) depending on taxable income

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Qualified dividends are taxed at the preferential 0%/15%/20% long-term capital gains rates, provided holding-period requirements are met. Why the others are wrong: **A** only nonqualified (ordinary) dividends are taxed at ordinary rates; **B** dividends are included in income, not excluded; **C** dividends are investment income, not subject to self-employment tax.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has a net capital loss of $9,000 for the year and no capital gains. How does this loss affect the individual's current-year return?

options.text: Up to $3,000 is deductible against ordinary income this year, and the remaining $6,000 carries forward
None of the loss is deductible until offset by future capital gains
The full $9,000 is deductible against ordinary income this year
The loss carries back three years before any current deduction

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An individual may deduct up to $3,000 of net capital losses against ordinary income each year, carrying the excess ($6,000) forward indefinitely. Why the others are wrong: **C** the annual deduction is capped at $3,000; **B** the $3,000 may be used currently against ordinary income; **D** individual capital losses carry forward, not back.

questions.stem: Which two items are generally treated as adjustments to arrive at adjusted gross income (above-the-line deductions) for an individual? (Select two.)

options.text: Deductible contributions to a traditional IRA
One-half of self-employment tax paid
State and local income taxes paid
Home mortgage interest on a primary residence

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Deductible traditional IRA contributions and one-half of self-employment tax are classic above-the-line adjustments that reduce gross income to AGI. Why the others are wrong: **D** home mortgage interest is an itemized (below-the-line) deduction on Schedule A; **C** state and local income taxes are itemized deductions (subject to the SALT cap), not adjustments.

questions.stem: An individual receives a pass-through loss from an entity. Place the three loss-limitation hurdles in the order they must be applied before any remaining loss can offset other income.

options.text: Tax-basis limitation
At-risk limitation
Passive activity loss limitation

questions.explanation: The hurdles apply in a fixed sequence: first the tax-basis limitation (a loss cannot exceed the owner's basis in the interest), then the at-risk limitation (the loss is further limited to amounts the owner has economically at risk), and finally the passive activity loss rules (a loss surviving the first two is deductible only against passive income, otherwise suspended). The order matters because each stage operates on the loss amount remaining after the prior stage, so applying them out of order yields the wrong deductible figure.

questions.stem: Which credit directly reduces a taxpayer's tax liability dollar-for-dollar and, in part, may be refundable for lower-income working taxpayers?

options.text: A mortgage interest itemized deduction
The standard deduction
The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
An adjustment for student loan interest

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Earned Income Tax Credit is a refundable credit that reduces tax dollar-for-dollar and can produce a refund for qualifying lower-income working taxpayers. Why the others are wrong: **B** the standard deduction reduces taxable income, not tax, and is not a credit; **D** student loan interest is an above-the-line deduction, not a credit; **A** mortgage interest is an itemized deduction, not a credit.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are tests that must be satisfied for a child to be claimed as a taxpayer's qualifying child? (Select two.)

options.text: The child must not have provided more than half of his or her own support
The child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half of the year
The child must have gross income below the exemption amount
The child must be a full-time student regardless of age

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The qualifying-child tests include the support test (the child does not provide more than half of his or her own support) and the residency test (the child lives with the taxpayer for more than half the year). Why the others are wrong: **C** the gross income test is a qualifying-relative test, not a qualifying-child test; **D** full-time student status only extends the age limit to under 24 — it is not itself a required test, and children under 19 qualify without being students.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an adjustment (preference or addback) commonly made in computing an individual's alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI)?

options.text: Adding back the state and local taxes deducted as itemized deductions for regular tax
Adding back qualified residence (home mortgage) interest used to buy a home
Subtracting all capital gains from AMTI
Adding back charitable contributions to public charities

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** State and local taxes deducted for regular tax are not allowed for AMT, so they are added back in computing AMTI. Why the others are wrong: **B** qualified residence interest used to acquire a home is generally still allowed for AMT; **D** charitable contributions remain deductible for AMT; **C** capital gains are taxed for AMT at the same preferential rates, not subtracted out.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder receives a Schedule K-1. Which statement about how the shareholder reports these items is correct?

options.text: All items are combined into a single ordinary income figure on the shareholder's return
Separately stated items (such as capital gains and charitable contributions) retain their character and are reported on the shareholder's return
Pass-through losses are always fully deductible regardless of the shareholder's basis
The shareholder reports only cash actually distributed, not the pass-through income

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Separately stated items pass through to S corporation shareholders and keep their character (e.g., long-term capital gain stays long-term) because they may be taxed differently at the shareholder level. Why the others are wrong: **A** items that must be separately stated cannot be lumped into ordinary income; **C** pass-through losses are limited by the shareholder's stock and debt basis; **D** pass-through income is taxed when earned, regardless of distributions.

questions.stem: Three individuals transfer property to a newly formed corporation solely in exchange for 100% of its stock. Immediately after the exchange they own all the stock. Under IRC §351, what is the general tax consequence of the transfer?

options.text: No gain or loss is recognized only if the corporation is an S corporation
Loss but not gain is recognized on the transfer
No gain or loss is recognized because the transferors are in control (at least 80%) immediately after the exchange
Gain is fully recognized because any transfer of appreciated property is taxable

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** IRC §351 provides nonrecognition when property is transferred solely for stock and the transferors collectively control the corporation (own at least 80% of voting power and stock) immediately after the exchange. Why the others are wrong: **D** the control requirement is met, so gain is deferred, not recognized; **B** §351 defers both gain and loss, not just loss; **A** §351 applies to corporate formations generally, not only S corporations.

questions.stem: On a C corporation's Schedule M-1, which two items are added to book income because they reduced book income but are not deductible (or are otherwise nondeductible) for tax? (Select two.)

options.text: Federal income tax expense recorded on the books
The nondeductible (50%) portion of business meals expense
Tax-exempt municipal bond interest income
Excess of MACRS tax depreciation over book depreciation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Federal income tax expense and the nondeductible portion of meals both reduce book income but are not deductible for tax, so each is added back on Schedule M-1 to reach taxable income. Why the others are wrong: **C** tax-exempt interest is in book income but not taxable, so it is a subtraction; **D** tax depreciation exceeding book depreciation is an extra tax deduction, also a subtraction, not an addition.

questions.stem: A C corporation owns 25% of the stock of a domestic taxable corporation from which it receives a dividend. Setting aside the taxable-income limitation, what dividends-received deduction (DRD) percentage generally applies?

options.text: 65%, because ownership is at least 20% but less than 80%
50%, because ownership is under 80%
100%, because any corporate shareholder gets a full deduction
0%, because corporations cannot deduct dividends received

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The DRD is 65% when the corporate recipient owns at least 20% but less than 80% of the payer. Why the others are wrong: **B** the 50% DRD applies to ownership below 20%, not the 20%-to-80% range; **C** the 100% DRD applies only when ownership is at least 80% (affiliated group); **D** corporations do receive a DRD to mitigate triple taxation.

questions.stem: Which of the following would disqualify a corporation from making or maintaining an S corporation election?

options.text: Having a single estate as a shareholder
Having a nonresident alien as a shareholder
Having 75 individual shareholders
Issuing a single class of common stock with identical rights

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An S corporation cannot have a nonresident alien shareholder; doing so terminates or prevents the election. Why the others are wrong: **C** an S corporation may have up to 100 shareholders, so 75 is fine; **A** estates are permitted S corporation shareholders; **D** an S corporation must have only one class of stock, so identical-rights common stock is allowed.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder has a stock basis of $20,000 at the beginning of the year. During the year the shareholder's share of ordinary business income is $8,000, tax-exempt income is $2,000, and a cash distribution of $5,000 is received. What is the shareholder's stock basis at year-end?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Stock basis increases for income items (including tax-exempt income) and decreases for distributions: $20,000 + $8,000 + $2,000 − $5,000 = $25,000. Why the others are wrong: **B** $23,000 wrongly omits the $2,000 tax-exempt income, which does increase basis; **A** $30,000 fails to subtract the $5,000 distribution; **D** $20,000 ignores all of the year's adjustments.

questions.stem: A partner contributes property with a fair market value of $50,000 and an adjusted basis of $30,000 to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. No liabilities are involved. Under the general partnership rules, what is the partner's basis in the partnership interest immediately after the contribution?

options.text: $20,000, the built-in gain on the property
$50,000, the fair market value of the contributed property
$0, because contributions to partnerships are always taxable
$30,000, the carryover (substituted) basis of the contributed property

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Under IRC §721 no gain is recognized on a contribution of property for a partnership interest, and the partner takes a substituted (carryover) outside basis equal to the property's adjusted basis of $30,000. Why the others are wrong: **B** FMV is not used for the partner's outside basis on a tax-free contribution; **A** $20,000 is the deferred built-in gain, not the basis; **C** §721 generally makes the contribution nontaxable, so basis is not zero.

questions.stem: By default, how is a domestic limited liability company (LLC) with two or more members classified for federal income tax purposes if it makes no entity-classification election?

options.text: As a partnership
As a disregarded entity
As an S corporation
As a C corporation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the check-the-box regulations, a domestic multi-member LLC that makes no election defaults to partnership taxation. Why the others are wrong: **D** the LLC is taxed as a C corporation only if it affirmatively elects corporate status on Form 8832; **C** S status additionally requires a separate election and eligibility; **B** disregarded-entity treatment is the default for a single-member LLC, not a multi-member LLC.

questions.stem: A C corporation distributes appreciated property (FMV $40,000; adjusted basis $15,000) to a shareholder as a dividend. The corporation has ample earnings and profits. What is the tax effect to the distributing corporation?

options.text: The corporation recognizes no gain because distributions are nontaxable to the distributor
The corporation recognizes a $25,000 gain as if it had sold the property at fair market value
The corporation deducts the $15,000 basis as a dividend expense
The corporation recognizes a $40,000 gain equal to the property's fair market value

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under IRC §311(b), a corporation distributing appreciated property recognizes gain as if it sold the property at FMV: $40,000 − $15,000 = $25,000 gain. Why the others are wrong: **A** distributions of appreciated property do trigger corporate-level gain; **D** the gain is the appreciation ($25,000), not the full FMV; **C** dividends are not deductible by the corporation, and basis is not 'expensed.'

questions.stem: An organization seeks federal tax-exempt status as a charitable organization under IRC §501(c)(3). Which activity would most jeopardize its exempt status?

options.text: Paying reasonable compensation to its employees
Receiving contributions from individual donors
Participating or intervening in a political campaign on behalf of a candidate for public office
Engaging in an insubstantial amount of unrelated business activity

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A §501(c)(3) organization is absolutely prohibited from participating or intervening in political campaigns for or against candidates; doing so can cost it its exemption. Why the others are wrong: **B** receiving donations is a normal, permitted activity; **A** paying reasonable (not excessive) compensation is allowed; **D** an insubstantial amount of unrelated business activity is tolerated (though its net income may be subject to UBIT), and does not by itself revoke exemption.

questions.stem: Which two items must generally be separately stated to partners on Schedule K-1 rather than included in the partnership's ordinary business income? (Select two.)

options.text: Cost of goods sold from ordinary operations
Salaries paid to non-partner employees
Net long-term capital gains and losses
Charitable contributions

questions.explanation: **Correct (C, D):** Items that could be taxed differently at the partner level — such as long-term capital gains/losses and charitable contributions — must be separately stated so each partner applies the correct rules. Why the others are wrong: **A** cost of goods sold is part of computing ordinary business income, not separately stated; **B** salaries to non-partner employees are an ordinary operating deduction, not separately stated.

questions.stem: A cash-method partner has an outside basis of $12,000 and receives a current (nonliquidating) cash distribution of $15,000. No partnership liabilities change. What is the tax effect to the partner?

options.text: The partner recognizes a $15,000 gain equal to the cash received
The partner recognizes a $12,000 loss equal to the prior basis
The partner recognizes no gain and reduces basis to negative $3,000
The partner recognizes a $3,000 gain to the extent cash exceeds outside basis, and basis becomes zero

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** In a current distribution, a partner recognizes gain only to the extent money received exceeds outside basis; here $15,000 − $12,000 = $3,000 gain, and basis is reduced to zero (never below zero). Why the others are wrong: **C** outside basis cannot go negative, so the excess is recognized as gain; **A** only the excess over basis, not the full distribution, is gain; **B** no loss is recognized on a current distribution.

questions.stem: A C corporation has a net operating loss (NOL) arising in tax year 2024. Under the rules applicable to NOLs arising after 2020, how may the corporation generally use this NOL?

options.text: Carry it forward indefinitely, offsetting up to 80% of taxable income in each carryforward year
Deduct it only in the year incurred, with no carryover permitted
Carry it back five years and offset 100% of income
Carry it back two years and forward twenty years without limitation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For NOLs arising in tax years after 2020, a corporation generally carries the loss forward indefinitely (no carryback) and may use it to offset up to 80% of taxable income in a given year. Why the others are wrong: **D** the old 2-back/20-forward, unlimited-offset regime was changed by the TCJA; **C** the five-year carryback was a temporary CARES Act rule for 2018–2020 NOLs only; **B** NOLs are carried over, not limited to the year incurred.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files a return on April 15, 2024. The IRS later wishes to assess additional tax. Absent fraud, a substantial omission of gross income, or a failure to file, what is the general statute of limitations for the IRS to assess additional tax?

options.text: Three years from the later of the due date or the date the return was filed
Six years from the date the return was filed
Ten years from the date the return was filed
There is no time limit on assessment

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under IRC §6501, the general assessment statute of limitations is three years from the later of the return's due date or its actual filing date. Why the others are wrong: **B** the six-year period applies only when there is a substantial (over 25%) omission of gross income; **C** ten years is the collection period after assessment, not the assessment period; **D** the unlimited period applies only to fraud or a failure to file a return.

questions.stem: A taxpayer fails to file a return by its due date and does not obtain an extension. The taxpayer owes tax and also pays it late. In a month in which both the failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties apply, how do they generally interact?

options.text: Both penalties apply at their full rate with no coordination
Neither penalty applies if the tax is eventually paid in full
Only the failure-to-pay penalty applies; the failure-to-file penalty is waived
The failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty for that month

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Under IRC §6651, when both penalties run in the same month, the 5%-per-month failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the 0.5%-per-month failure-to-pay penalty, so the combined charge is 5% for that month. Why the others are wrong: **A** the statute expressly coordinates them rather than stacking both fully; **C** the failure-to-file penalty is not waived merely because a payment penalty also runs; **B** late payment and late filing still incur penalties even if the balance is later paid.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid a disputed tax in full and now wishes to sue for a refund and to demand a jury trial. In which forum must the taxpayer file?

options.text: The U.S. Tax Court
The U.S. Court of Federal Claims
The U.S. District Court
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Of the federal trial forums, only the U.S. District Court offers a jury trial, and like the Court of Federal Claims it is a refund forum requiring the tax to be paid first. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Tax Court hears cases without prepayment but never empanels a jury; **B** the Court of Federal Claims is a refund forum but decides cases without a jury; **D** the Federal Circuit is an appellate court, not a trial forum.

questions.stem: Under the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services, when may a CPA in tax practice rely on information furnished by the client without verifying it?

options.text: Never; the CPA must independently verify all client-supplied data
Only if the client provides audited financial statements
Only after obtaining a written representation letter from the client's attorney
The CPA may rely in good faith on client information without verification, but must make reasonable inquiries if it appears incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** SSTS No. 2 permits a CPA to rely in good faith on information the client furnishes, without verification, but requires reasonable inquiry when the information appears incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent. Why the others are wrong: **A** the standard does not impose a duty to audit or verify every figure; **B** audited statements are not a precondition to reliance; **C** an attorney's representation letter is not required to accept routine client data.

questions.stem: Under Treasury Circular 230, the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) finds that a CPA willfully violated the regulations. Which sanction is OPR authorized to impose?

options.text: Revocation of the CPA's state-issued license to practice public accounting
Imprisonment of the practitioner for up to one year
Censure, suspension, or disbarment from practice before the IRS, and a monetary penalty
An order requiring the CPA to pay the client's additional tax

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Circular 230 §10.50 empowers the IRS (through OPR) to censure, suspend, or disbar a practitioner from practice before the IRS and to impose a monetary penalty. Why the others are wrong: **A** only the state board of accountancy, not OPR, can revoke a CPA license; **B** OPR imposes administrative sanctions, not criminal imprisonment; **D** OPR cannot order a practitioner to pay a client's tax liability.

questions.stem: A taxpayer asserts the reasonable-cause and good-faith defense to avoid an accuracy-related penalty. Which two factors support a reasonable-cause defense? (Select two.)

options.text: The taxpayer reasonably relied in good faith on the advice of a competent tax professional given all necessary facts
The taxpayer made an honest effort to determine the correct tax and exercised ordinary business care
The taxpayer was unaware that the income was taxable but kept no records
The taxpayer chose not to file because paying the tax would be inconvenient

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Reasonable cause under IRC §6664 turns on good-faith reliance on competent professional advice (with full disclosure of the facts) and on the taxpayer's exercise of ordinary business care and prudence. Why the others are wrong: **C** a bare claim of ignorance without recordkeeping does not establish reasonable care; **D** mere inconvenience or unwillingness to pay is not reasonable cause and shows a lack of good faith.

questions.stem: An agent acting within the scope of authority enters into a contract for a disclosed principal, signing in the principal's name. The third party later sues for breach. Who is generally liable on the contract?

options.text: The agent alone, because the agent signed the contract
The principal alone, because the principal was disclosed and the agent acted within authority
Both the agent and the principal jointly and severally
Neither, because a disclosed-principal contract is unenforceable

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When an authorized agent contracts for a fully disclosed principal, the principal is bound and the agent is not personally liable. Why the others are wrong: **A** signing on behalf of a disclosed principal does not make the agent a party; **C** joint liability typically arises with an undisclosed or partially disclosed principal, not a fully disclosed one; **D** the contract is enforceable—against the principal.

questions.stem: A homeowner contracts with a builder to remodel a kitchen. The builder completes the work but installs a different brand of faucet of equal quality and the project is otherwise complete and usable. Under common law, how is the builder's performance best characterized?

options.text: A material breach that excuses the homeowner from all payment
An anticipatory repudiation by the builder
Substantial performance, entitling the builder to the contract price less damages for the minor deviation
A perfect tender that bars any offset to the homeowner

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A minor, non-willful deviation that leaves the project complete and usable is substantial performance; the builder recovers the contract price reduced by damages for the defect. Why the others are wrong: **A** a trivial deviation is not a material breach and does not excuse all payment; **B** repudiation requires a clear refusal to perform, which did not occur; **D** the perfect-tender rule applies to the sale of goods under the UCC, not to construction services.

questions.stem: A debtor defaults, and three creditors hold security interests in the same equipment: Creditor X perfected by filing on March 1; Creditor Y's interest attached February 1 but remains unperfected; Creditor Z perfected by filing on April 1. Under UCC Article 9, what is the priority order?

options.text: Y, then X, then Z, because Y's interest attached first
Z, then X, then Y, because the most recent filing controls
All three share pro rata because they cover the same collateral
X, then Z, then Y, because perfected interests outrank unperfected ones and rank by filing date

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Among competing security interests, perfected interests beat unperfected ones, and perfected interests rank by the first to file or perfect; thus X (March 1) beats Z (April 1), and both beat the unperfected Y. Why the others are wrong: **A** an earlier attachment does not give an unperfected creditor priority over perfected creditors; **B** priority runs from the earliest filing, not the latest; **C** Article 9 establishes a priority ladder rather than pro rata sharing.

questions.stem: An investor sues an issuer under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933, alleging a material misstatement in a registration statement. Which statement about the plaintiff's burden is correct?

options.text: The plaintiff must prove the issuer acted with scienter (intent to deceive)
The plaintiff must prove reliance on the misstatement in every case
The plaintiff need only show a material misstatement or omission and damages; the issuer is essentially liable without a due-diligence defense
The plaintiff must prove privity of contract with the issuer

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Under Section 11, a plaintiff need only show a material misstatement or omission in the registration statement and a resulting loss; the issuer has essentially no due-diligence defense (though other defendants do). Why the others are wrong: **A** Section 11 does not require proof of scienter, unlike Rule 10b-5; **B** reliance generally need not be shown (with a narrow exception after a long post-effective period); **D** privity is not required—purchasers in the offering may sue.

questions.stem: A shareholder of a C corporation wishes to hold directors personally accountable for a decision that caused a loss. The directors made the decision in good faith, on an informed basis, and without a conflict of interest. Under the business judgment rule, what is the likely result?

options.text: The directors are personally liable for any loss the corporation suffers
The directors are automatically liable unless the decision was unanimous
The shareholder may recover only if the corporation was insolvent
The directors are protected from liability because they acted in good faith, were informed, and had no conflict

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The business judgment rule shields directors from liability for honest, informed, disinterested decisions, even if those decisions turn out badly. Why the others are wrong: **A** directors are not insurers of corporate success and are not liable for good-faith business judgments; **B** unanimity is not required for the protection to apply; **C** the rule protects directors regardless of the corporation's solvency, absent a breach of duty.

questions.stem: A buyer of goods receives a shipment that fails to conform to the contract in a single-delivery (non-installment) sale. Under the UCC perfect tender rule, what may the buyer generally do?

options.text: Only accept the goods and sue for damages; rejection is not permitted
Reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest
Reject only if the nonconformity is material and substantial
Keep the goods without paying because the seller breached

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under UCC §2-601's perfect tender rule, if goods fail to conform in any respect the buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest. Why the others are wrong: **C** the material-breach threshold governs common-law contracts and UCC installment contracts, not a single-delivery sale; **A** rejection is an available remedy; **D** an accepting buyer must pay the contract price (subject to offset for damages).

questions.stem: A surety pays a creditor in full after the principal debtor defaults. Which two rights does the surety generally have? (Select two.)

options.text: Reimbursement (indemnity) from the principal debtor
Subrogation to the creditor's rights against the principal debtor
The right to keep the collateral free of any duty to account to co-sureties
The right to compel the creditor to refund amounts the surety never paid

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A surety who pays the debt may seek reimbursement from the principal debtor and is subrogated to the creditor's rights and remedies against that debtor. Why the others are wrong: **C** a paying surety owes co-sureties a right of contribution and must account, not keep collateral free of that duty; **D** the surety cannot demand a refund of amounts it did not actually pay.

questions.stem: An individual debtor files for bankruptcy and seeks a discharge of debts. Which of the following obligations is generally NOT dischargeable in bankruptcy?

options.text: Unsecured credit card balances
Amounts owed to trade suppliers on open account
A deficiency remaining after repossession of personal property
Most recent federal income taxes and domestic support (alimony/child support) obligations

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Recent taxes and domestic support obligations such as alimony and child support are excepted from discharge under the Bankruptcy Code. Why the others are wrong: **A** ordinary unsecured credit card debt is generally dischargeable; **B** open-account trade debt is typically dischargeable; **C** an unsecured deficiency after repossession is generally dischargeable like other unsecured debt.

questions.stem: On July 1 of tax year 2024, a business places in service a new piece of machinery (7-year MACRS property) costing $100,000 and elects no bonus depreciation or Section 179. Which MACRS convention generally applies, assuming under 40% of the year's property was placed in service in the fourth quarter?

options.text: The half-year convention, treating the property as placed in service at the midpoint of the year
The mid-month convention, treating it as placed in service mid-July
The mid-quarter convention for all personal property
A full-year convention, allowing a full year of depreciation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** MACRS personal property generally uses the half-year convention, treating assets as placed in service at the year's midpoint, unless the mid-quarter convention is triggered. Why the others are wrong: **C** the mid-quarter convention applies only when more than 40% of personal property is placed in service in the last quarter, which is not the case here; **B** the mid-month convention is used for real property, not machinery; **D** MACRS never grants a full year in the placed-in-service year for such property.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's business building is destroyed by fire. The taxpayer receives $500,000 of insurance proceeds (realizing a $200,000 gain) and, within the replacement period, reinvests $460,000 in a qualifying replacement building. Under the Section 1033 involuntary conversion rules, how much gain must the taxpayer recognize?

options.text: $0, because all involuntary conversion gains are permanently excluded
$200,000, the entire realized gain
$460,000, the amount reinvested
$40,000, the amount of proceeds not reinvested

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Under §1033, gain is recognized to the extent the proceeds exceed the cost of qualifying replacement property; $500,000 − $460,000 = $40,000 not reinvested, which is recognized (capped at the $200,000 realized gain). Why the others are wrong: **B** reinvesting most of the proceeds defers gain, so the full gain is not recognized; **A** §1033 defers rather than permanently excludes gain; **C** the reinvested amount is not the measure of recognized gain.

questions.stem: An individual sells a capital asset for a gain. The asset was acquired on March 10, 2023, and sold on March 10, 2024. How is the holding period and resulting gain best characterized?

options.text: Short-term, because the asset was not held more than one year
Long-term, because the asset was held more than one year
Short-term, because the holding period always excludes the year of sale
Long-term, because any asset held into a second calendar year is long-term

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Long-term treatment requires holding the asset more than one year; the holding period begins the day after acquisition (March 11, 2023) and a sale on March 10, 2024 is exactly one year, which is not more than one year, so the gain is short-term. Why the others are wrong: **B** a holding period of exactly one year fails the 'more than one year' test; **D** crossing into a new calendar year does not by itself create long-term status; **C** the holding period is measured by days held, not by excluding the sale year.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells depreciable real property (a building) used in a trade or business at a gain. Which two statements about depreciation recapture on the building are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: Section 1250 generally recaptures as ordinary income only depreciation taken in excess of straight-line
Because straight-line MACRS is used for real property, there is typically no Section 1250 ordinary recapture
The entire gain is always recaptured as ordinary income like Section 1245 property
Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain attributable to prior straight-line depreciation may be taxed to individuals at a maximum 25% rate

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** Because real property is depreciated using straight-line MACRS, there is no excess over straight-line, so §1250 produces little or no ordinary recapture; instead, the prior straight-line depreciation creates 'unrecaptured §1250 gain' taxed to individuals at a maximum 25% rate. Why the others are wrong: **A** §1250 recaptures the excess over straight-line, but with straight-line MACRS there is no such excess; **C** real property is not treated like §1245 property with full recapture of all gain.

questions.stem: A cash-basis individual receives a $5,000 check from a customer on December 30, 2024, but does not deposit or cash it until January 3, 2025. Under the constructive receipt doctrine, in which year is the $5,000 included in gross income?

options.text: 2024, because the income was available without substantial limitation in that year
2025, because the funds were not deposited until then
Split evenly between 2024 and 2025
Neither year, because checks are not income until cashed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under constructive receipt, income is taxed when it is made available without substantial restriction; the customer's check received in 2024 is income in 2024 even if deposited later. Why the others are wrong: **B** delaying the deposit does not defer the income for a cash-basis taxpayer; **C** there is no proration of a single payment across years; **D** a check available to the payee is constructively received and is income when received.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives a state income tax refund in 2024 attributable to 2023. In 2023, the taxpayer claimed the standard deduction rather than itemizing. How is the 2024 refund treated?

options.text: It is fully taxable as gross income in 2024
It is excluded from income under the tax benefit rule because no deduction was claimed for it
It is taxable only to the extent it exceeds $1,000
It must be carried back and reported on the 2023 return

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the tax benefit rule, a state tax refund is taxable only if the taxpayer received a tax benefit by deducting those taxes; because the taxpayer took the standard deduction in 2023, the refund yields no prior benefit and is excluded. Why the others are wrong: **A** the refund is not automatically taxable when no deduction benefit was obtained; **C** there is no $1,000 threshold; **D** the refund is reported (if at all) in the year received, not carried back.

questions.stem: For tax year 2024, an individual incurs $12,000 of unreimbursed qualified medical expenses and has adjusted gross income of $100,000. If the taxpayer itemizes, how much of the medical expense is deductible?

options.text: $12,000, the full amount paid
$4,500, the amount exceeding 7.5% of AGI
$2,000, the amount exceeding 10% of AGI
$0, because medical expenses are never deductible

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI; 7.5% of $100,000 is $7,500, so $12,000 − $7,500 = $4,500 is deductible. Why the others are wrong: **C** the floor is 7.5% of AGI, not 10%; **A** the full amount is not deductible because the AGI floor reduces it; **D** qualifying medical expenses above the floor are deductible by itemizers.

questions.stem: A married couple filing jointly has two qualifying children under age 17 and modified AGI of $150,000 for tax year 2024, well below the phase-out threshold. Regarding the Child Tax Credit, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The credit is fully refundable in all cases up to the full per-child amount
The credit is available only if the children have no earned income of their own
The credit phases out beginning at $50,000 of modified AGI for joint filers
The credit is a per-qualifying-child credit that is partially refundable (as the additional child tax credit) subject to an earned-income-based limit

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Child Tax Credit is a per-qualifying-child credit that is only partially refundable through the additional child tax credit, with refundability limited by a percentage of earned income above a threshold. Why the others are wrong: **A** the credit is not fully refundable; only a capped portion is refundable; **C** for joint filers the phase-out begins at $400,000 of modified AGI, not $50,000; **B** a child's own earned income is not a disqualifier for the credit.

questions.stem: A self-employed individual reports net earnings from self-employment for tax year 2024. Which statement about self-employment (SE) tax is correct?

options.text: SE tax is imposed on 100% of net self-employment earnings with no adjustment
SE tax is fully deductible as an itemized deduction
SE tax consists only of the Social Security portion, with no Medicare component
SE tax applies to 92.35% of net self-employment earnings, and one-half of the SE tax is deductible above the line

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** SE tax is computed on 92.35% of net self-employment earnings, and the taxpayer deducts one-half of the SE tax as an above-the-line adjustment. Why the others are wrong: **A** the base is 92.35%, not 100%, of net earnings; **C** SE tax includes both Social Security (capped) and Medicare (uncapped) components; **B** the deductible half is an adjustment to income, not an itemized deduction.

questions.stem: An individual operates a qualifying business and considers the qualified business income (QBI) deduction under Section 199A. The taxpayer's taxable income is below the threshold at which limitations apply. What is the general QBI deduction?

options.text: 20% of qualified business income (subject to an overall limit based on taxable income less net capital gain)
50% of W-2 wages paid by the business in all cases
A deduction equal to the full amount of qualified business income
A credit equal to 20% of qualified business income

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The §199A deduction is generally 20% of qualified business income, limited to 20% of taxable income less net capital gain; below the threshold, the W-2 wage/property limits do not apply. Why the others are wrong: **B** the W-2 wage limitation applies only above the taxable-income threshold; **C** the deduction is 20% of QBI, not the entire QBI; **D** §199A is a deduction, not a credit.

questions.stem: A taxpayer pays $3,000 of qualified education expenses for a dependent's first year of college and wishes to maximize an education benefit. Which statement about the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) is correct?

options.text: It is available for an unlimited number of years of post-secondary education
It is a deduction from gross income, not a credit
It applies to the first four years of post-secondary education, is partially refundable, and covers 100% of the first $2,000 plus 25% of the next $2,000 of qualified expenses
It can be claimed in the same year as the Lifetime Learning Credit for the same student's same expenses

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The AOTC covers the first four years of post-secondary education, equals 100% of the first $2,000 plus 25% of the next $2,000 of qualified expenses (max $2,500), and is 40% refundable. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is limited to four years, unlike the Lifetime Learning Credit; **D** the AOTC and Lifetime Learning Credit cannot both be claimed for the same student's same expenses in the same year; **B** it is a credit, not a deduction.

questions.stem: Which two items are generally deductible as itemized deductions on an individual's Schedule A (subject to applicable limits)? (Select two.)

options.text: Charitable contributions to qualified organizations
State and local taxes, subject to the SALT deduction cap
Commuting costs from home to a regular workplace
Personal credit card interest

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Charitable contributions to qualified organizations and state and local taxes (subject to the SALT deduction cap) are itemized deductions on Schedule A. Why the others are wrong: **C** commuting between home and a regular workplace is a nondeductible personal expense; **D** personal (consumer) interest such as credit card interest is not deductible.

questions.stem: A grandparent contributes to a Section 529 qualified tuition program for a grandchild. Earnings in the account are later used for the beneficiary's qualified higher education expenses. How are those earnings treated for federal income tax?

options.text: Earnings are taxable to the contributor each year as they accrue
Earnings grow tax-deferred and distributions are tax-free if used for qualified education expenses
Earnings are always subject to a 10% penalty when withdrawn
Contributions are deductible on the federal return and earnings are taxed at distribution

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In a §529 plan, earnings grow tax-deferred and qualified distributions used for qualified education expenses are excluded from federal income tax. Why the others are wrong: **A** earnings are not taxed annually as they accrue; **C** the 10% penalty applies only to the earnings portion of nonqualified distributions; **D** contributions are not deductible federally, though qualified distributions are tax-free.

questions.stem: An individual sells stock at a $4,000 loss on November 10 and repurchases substantially identical stock on November 25 of the same year. Under the wash sale rules, what is the federal income tax consequence?

options.text: The $4,000 loss is currently deductible because the sale was a bona fide disposition
The $4,000 loss is permanently lost with no basis adjustment
The $4,000 loss is disallowed and added to the basis of the replacement stock
Only half of the loss is disallowed because the repurchase occurred within 30 days

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A wash sale occurs when substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after a loss sale; the loss is disallowed currently and added to the basis of the replacement shares. Why the others are wrong: **A** the loss is not currently deductible because of the repurchase; **B** the disallowed loss is preserved through a basis increase, not permanently lost; **D** the entire loss is disallowed, not just half.

questions.stem: An individual exercises an incentive stock option (ISO) and holds the shares at year-end without selling. For regular tax there is no income on exercise. What is the alternative minimum tax (AMT) consequence in the year of exercise?

options.text: There is no AMT consequence because ISOs are never an AMT item
The bargain element (FMV at exercise less the strike price) is a positive AMT adjustment in the year of exercise
The entire fair market value of the shares is ordinary income for AMT
The strike price is added back as an AMT preference

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** For ISOs, the bargain element (FMV at exercise minus the exercise price) is a positive AMT adjustment in the exercise year, even though it is not regular-tax income until sale. Why the others are wrong: **A** the ISO bargain element is a classic AMT item; **C** only the bargain element, not the full FMV, is the adjustment; **D** it is the spread, not the strike price itself, that is added for AMT.

questions.stem: A C corporation accumulates earnings beyond the reasonable needs of its business to avoid shareholder-level tax on dividends. Which federal tax may apply at the corporate level?

options.text: The accumulated earnings tax
The self-employment tax
The dividends-received deduction recapture
The generation-skipping transfer tax

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The accumulated earnings tax is a penalty tax on a C corporation that retains earnings beyond its reasonable business needs to help shareholders avoid dividend taxation. Why the others are wrong: **B** self-employment tax applies to individuals' net earnings, not corporations; **C** there is no 'DRD recapture' tax for accumulating earnings; **D** the generation-skipping transfer tax applies to certain transfers, not corporate accumulations.

questions.stem: A closely held C corporation has few shareholders and substantial passive investment income. It is classified as a personal holding company (PHC). What is the consequence if it does not distribute its income?

options.text: It loses its corporate status and is taxed as a partnership
An additional personal holding company tax is imposed on undistributed PHC income
Its shareholders are taxed immediately on all corporate earnings
It must immediately liquidate under federal law

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A personal holding company is subject to an additional PHC tax on its undistributed personal holding company income, encouraging distribution of passive earnings. Why the others are wrong: **A** PHC status does not convert the entity to a partnership; **C** shareholders are not automatically taxed on undistributed corporate earnings; **D** there is no forced liquidation—the corporation simply faces the additional tax.

questions.stem: A C corporation makes a cash distribution to a shareholder. The corporation has accumulated earnings and profits (E&P) but a current-year deficit, and after applying E&P rules the distribution exceeds total E&P. How is the portion exceeding E&P treated to the shareholder?

options.text: As a dividend to the full extent of the distribution
As ordinary compensation income
As a nontaxable return of capital reducing stock basis, then as capital gain to the extent it exceeds basis
As tax-exempt income with no basis effect

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A corporate distribution is a dividend only to the extent of E&P; the excess is first a tax-free return of capital that reduces stock basis, and any amount beyond basis is capital gain. Why the others are wrong: **A** only the portion covered by E&P is a dividend; **B** a distribution on stock is not compensation; **D** the excess is not tax-exempt—it reduces basis and can generate capital gain.

questions.stem: An S corporation that was formerly a C corporation has accumulated earnings and profits from its C years and, for three consecutive years, has passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts. What is the consequence?

options.text: Nothing, because S corporations are never affected by passive income
The S election terminates after the third consecutive year, and an entity-level tax on excess net passive income may apply in the interim
The corporation must immediately convert to a partnership
All shareholders lose their stock basis

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An S corporation with C-corporation E&P that has excess passive investment income (over 25% of gross receipts) for three consecutive years loses its S election, and a separate entity-level tax on excess net passive income can apply in those years. Why the others are wrong: **A** S corporations with C-era E&P are subject to these passive income rules; **C** termination reverts the entity to C-corporation status, not a partnership; **D** the rule does not eliminate shareholder basis.

questions.stem: A partner has an outside basis of $10,000 in a partnership and is allocated a $40,000 share of partnership recourse liabilities. The partner's share of liabilities then decreases by $15,000 due to debt repayment. How does the $15,000 decrease affect the partner?

options.text: It has no effect on the partner's outside basis
It increases the partner's outside basis by $15,000
It is treated as a deemed cash distribution that reduces the partner's outside basis
It is treated as ordinary income of $15,000

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Under §752, a decrease in a partner's share of partnership liabilities is treated as a deemed cash distribution that reduces the partner's outside basis (and can trigger gain if it exceeds basis). Why the others are wrong: **B** an increase in liability share—not a decrease—raises basis; **A** liability changes do affect outside basis; **D** the deemed distribution reduces basis and is not automatically ordinary income.

questions.stem: A guaranteed payment is made to a partner for services rendered to the partnership, determined without regard to partnership income. How is the guaranteed payment treated?

options.text: As a nondeductible distribution to the partner with no effect on partnership income
As a tax-free return of capital to the partner
As a dividend taxed at preferential capital gains rates
As ordinary income to the receiving partner and generally deductible (or capitalizable) by the partnership in computing its income

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A guaranteed payment for services, set without regard to partnership income, is ordinary income to the partner and is generally deductible (or capitalized) by the partnership when figuring its taxable income. Why the others are wrong: **A** guaranteed payments do affect partnership income because they are deductible/capitalizable; **B** they are compensation, not a return of capital; **C** they are ordinary income, not preferentially taxed dividends.

questions.stem: A tax-exempt organization that is otherwise exempt operates a business regularly carried on that is unrelated to its exempt purpose. How is the net income from that activity generally treated?

options.text: It is always exempt because the organization itself is tax-exempt
It is taxed to the organization's individual donors
It is subject to the unrelated business income tax (UBIT) at corporate income tax rates
It causes automatic revocation of exempt status regardless of amount

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Net income from a regularly carried-on trade or business unrelated to the exempt purpose is subject to the unrelated business income tax (UBIT), generally at corporate rates. Why the others are wrong: **A** unrelated business income is not shielded by the organization's exempt status; **B** the tax falls on the organization, not its donors; **D** an insubstantial amount of unrelated activity does not automatically revoke exemption—only its net income is taxed.

questions.stem: On a C corporation's Schedule M-1, the corporation reconciles book income to taxable income. Tax-exempt municipal bond interest of $5,000 is included in book income. How is this item handled on Schedule M-1?

options.text: It is added to book income to reach taxable income
It has no effect because it appears on neither the books nor the return
It is added to taxable income because tax-exempt interest is fully taxable to corporations
It is subtracted from book income because it is included in book income but is not taxable

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Tax-exempt interest is part of book income but is excluded from taxable income, so on Schedule M-1 it is subtracted from book income when reconciling to taxable income. Why the others are wrong: **A** subtracting, not adding, reflects income that is in the books but not taxable; **C** municipal bond interest is not taxable to corporations; **B** the item is in book income, so it must be removed in the reconciliation.

questions.stem: Which two items decrease a partner's outside basis in a partnership interest? (Select two.)

options.text: The partner's distributive share of partnership losses and nondeductible expenses
Cash distributions received from the partnership
